item.title: Won at the Supreme Court, Still Waiting on the Check: Inside the $165 Billion Tariff Refund Nobody Can Collect
item.body:
There is a peculiar kind of legal victory in which you win everything and receive nothing. Somewhere around 330,000 American importers are living in it right now.

Six months after the Supreme Court held, 6–3, that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not give any president the authority to impose tariffs, the courts have ordered roughly $165 billion in collected duties returned to the companies that paid them. On paper, that is one of the largest single refund events the U.S. Treasury has ever faced. In practice, most of the businesses entitled to that money have not seen a dollar of it — and a large share of them are still cutting tariff checks every week.

The gap between the ruling and the refund is not a scandal. It is plumbing. But the plumbing is worth understanding, because it explains why a landmark constitutional decision has so far changed far less about the cost of importing goods into the United States than the headline suggested.

## What the Court actually decided

IEEPA, passed in 1977, lets a president declare a national emergency in response to an "unusual and extraordinary threat" originating largely outside the United States, and then take a list of economic actions — among them, the authority to "regulate ... importation."

The government's argument rested on those three words. If you can regulate importation, the reasoning went, you can condition importation on payment of a duty. Emergencies are unpredictable, and Congress wrote the statute broadly on purpose.

The challengers — a group of small importers and a coalition of states, whose cases were consolidated on the way up — made a structural argument instead. The power to lay duties belongs to Congress under Article I. IEEPA never uses the words *tariff*, *duty*, or *tax*. And in nearly fifty years, across administrations of both parties, no president had ever read the statute that way.

The majority sided with the challengers, applying the now-familiar principle that Congress does not hide decisions of vast economic and political significance inside vague or ancillary statutory language. The Court noted something telling: when Congress *has* delegated tariff authority, it has done so deliberately and with guardrails — required investigations, agency findings, rate ceilings, sunset clauses. IEEPA has none of those. The absence of any procedural machinery was treated as evidence that the machinery was never meant to be there.

The dissent argued for deference in the field of foreign affairs, and read "regulate importation" as plainly capacious enough to include a tariff.

One point gets lost in the coverage: the decision is about *which branch* sets tariffs and *under which statute*. It is not a ruling on whether tariffs are wise policy. That distinction explains nearly everything that has happened since.

## Why winning is not the same as being paid

Customs refunds do not work like a court-ordered settlement where a check gets mailed. They work entry by entry, through a system built for correcting individual paperwork errors, not for unwinding a policy applied to tens of millions of shipments.

**Liquidation is the deadline nobody outside the trade world had heard of.** When goods enter the United States, the importer files an entry summary and deposits estimated duties. Months later, Customs and Border Protection "liquidates" the entry — the final, legally binding computation of what was owed. Once an entry liquidates and the protest window closes, it is generally final. Reopening it requires a specific legal hook. Many entries from the tariffs' earliest months liquidated long before the case reached the Supreme Court, and a meaningful slice of the theoretical $165 billion sits behind that door.

**Being right is not the same as being a party.** Court orders run to the parties before the court. Whether relief extends automatically to every importer in the country, or whether each company must file its own protest or suit to claim its share, has been litigated separately — and that secondary fight is where a great deal of the money is currently parked. Importers who filed protective claims early are in a materially better position than those who waited for the news.

**The refund itself is an accounting exercise at enormous scale.** CBP processes tens of millions of entry summaries a year. Each refund has to be matched to a specific entry, a specific line, a specific tariff classification, and often a specific surety bond. Some entries mixed duties that are now void with duties that remain perfectly valid under other statutes. Untangling those lines is manual work, and there is no button that does it.

**Interest accrues, which softens the wait but complicates the math.** Excess deposits generally carry interest from the date of deposit until refund, at rates Treasury resets quarterly. For a company that paid millions in 2025, that is real money — and also a taxable event landing in a different fiscal year than the original expense.

**Appeals and remands keep resetting the clock.** Even after a Supreme Court ruling on the core question, the downstream cases about scope, timing, and eligibility continue to move through the Court of International Trade and the Federal Circuit. Every remand adds months.

## Who actually gets the money

This is the question that produces the most awkward conversations inside companies.

The refund goes to the **importer of record** — the entity legally on the hook to CBP. That is often not the party that ultimately bore the cost. A U.S. distributor that paid the duty and raised its prices has already recovered much of it from customers. A retailer that negotiated delivered-duty-paid terms may have pushed the cost onto a foreign supplier. Some contracts contain explicit tariff-adjustment clauses that now run in reverse; most do not.

The result is a wave of quiet commercial negotiation that has nothing to do with the constitutional question: *who, in this supply chain, owns this receivable?* Companies with clean documentation and well-drafted clauses are resolving it in weeks. Companies without are discovering that a windfall is only a windfall if you can prove it is yours.

## The wall that replaced the wall

Here is the part that surprises people who followed only the headline. For many importers, the total duty burden has not fallen much, because the tariffs did not disappear so much as change legal address.

IEEPA was the fast lane. Everything else is slower, narrower, and procedurally demanding — but it exists, and it has been used.

| Authority | What it requires | Practical constraints |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Section 232** (Trade Expansion Act of 1962) | Commerce Department investigation finding that imports threaten national security | Product-by-product; investigations take months; no statutory rate cap |
| **Section 301** (Trade Act of 1974) | USTR investigation into unfair foreign practices | Country-specific; notice-and-comment; subject to periodic review |
| **Section 201** (Trade Act of 1974) | ITC finding of serious injury to a domestic industry | Temporary safeguard; must phase down over time |
| **Section 122** (Trade Act of 1974) | Balance-of-payments justification | Capped at 15% and 150 days without congressional action |

Section 232 has done most of the work. Because it is organized around product categories rather than countries, rebuilding coverage means running investigations sector by sector — steel and aluminum derivatives, autos and parts, copper, timber and lumber, pharmaceuticals, semiconductors and downstream electronics. Each one is a separate proceeding with its own comment docket and its own effective date.

The practical effect for an importer is that a refund for last year's duties can arrive in the same quarter as a new invoice for this year's, on the same product, at a comparable rate, under a different statute. The money is real. The relief is not.

## What it means for the books

Accountants have been unusually vocal about this one. Under U.S. GAAP, gain contingencies generally are not recognized until realized or realizable — so a company cannot simply book its expected refund as an asset because it read a favorable opinion. The original tariffs were typically expensed through cost of goods sold or capitalized into inventory. The refunds, when they land, tend to arrive as a lump in a later period, distorting margins in a quarter that had nothing to do with the shipments in question.

That timing mismatch is why some importers with large confirmed claims still look, on paper, like they are absorbing tariff costs. They are — until the money moves.

## What it means for prices

Prices are famously sticky downward. Costs that got passed to consumers over two years do not reverse on the day a court rules, particularly when replacement duties are landing in the same categories. Where relief has shown up fastest is in goods that fell outside every Section 232 product scope — certain consumer categories, some apparel and household goods, various inputs with no plausible national-security framing. Where it has shown up least is anywhere touching metals, vehicles, electronics, or pharmaceuticals.

## What to watch next

- **The scope litigation.** Whether relief reaches non-parties automatically is worth more, in dollars, than most of the underlying case.
- **The liquidation cutoff rulings.** Courts are being asked whether finality bars claims on entries that liquidated before the decision. This is the single largest variable in the $165 billion estimate.
- **CBP's processing pace.** Refund throughput, not legal entitlement, now sets the calendar for most companies.
- **New Section 232 proceedings.** Each new product scope narrows the practical benefit of the refund for affected importers.
- **Congress.** The decision hands tariff-setting back to the legislature by default. Whether Congress legislates new delegated authority, tightens the existing ones, or does nothing will determine what the next version of this looks like.

## A practical checklist for importers

If your company imported during the affected period, the useful steps are unglamorous:

1. **Pull your entry data.** Identify every entry summary in the window and its liquidation status. You cannot claim what you cannot locate.
2. **Preserve rights on unliquidated entries** through the appropriate protest or post-summary correction channels, with customs counsel, before deadlines pass.
3. **Separate voided duties from valid ones** line by line. Mixed entries are the most common source of rejected claims.
4. **Read your contracts** for tariff pass-through and adjustment clauses, in both directions, before anyone assumes the refund is theirs.
5. **Talk to your auditor early** about recognition timing so the refund does not become a surprise restatement conversation.
6. **Model the replacement duties**, not the old ones. Your forward cost curve depends on Section 232 scopes, not on a case you already won.

## Bottom line

The Supreme Court answered a constitutional question cleanly: an emergency-powers statute that never mentions tariffs does not authorize them. What it could not do is make an administrative system built for correcting individual entry errors process a nationwide reversal quickly, or prevent the executive branch from rebuilding similar duties through statutes that were always available and are now being used.

For 330,000 companies, the ruling converted a cost into a receivable. That is a genuine improvement. It is also a reminder that in trade law, the judgment is the beginning of the process, not the end of it — and that the distance between a court order and a bank deposit is measured in liquidation dates, not in principles.

---

*This article is general information, not legal, tax, or accounting advice. Figures cited are estimates that shift as litigation and refund processing continue. Importers with potential claims should consult licensed customs counsel and their own advisors about their specific entries and deadlines.*
